2 Samuel 24 · David Numbers Israel and Buys the Threshing Floor

precepts.text: Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number Israel; this is the precept showing how the Most High used Satan to accomplish his judgment.
precepts.point: Notwithstanding, the king's word prevailed against Joab and the captains, and they went out to number the people. Joab did not understand that behind it all, verse one, the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel; it was of the Most High that this happened.

note.label: 2 Samuel 24: David Numbers Israel and Buys the Threshing Floor

precepts.why:
The same story told in Chronicles names who stood behind the numbering: “And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel.” Second Samuel says the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel and “he moved David against them”; Chronicles says Satan provoked him. Both are true.

The Most High wanted to judge Israel, and he used Satan to provoke David to do it. That is how he accomplished his judgment. The numbering was not the king's job but the work of the Levites, which is why Joab asked, “why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?”

Notwithstanding, “the king’s word prevailed against Joab”, and the captains went out to number the people. Joab did not see what was behind it all: verse one, “the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel.” It was of the Most High that this happened.

precepts.text: David would not offer to the Most High that which cost him nothing, the same conviction that made him pay the full price.
precepts.point: David paid the full price rather than take the offering for free, and this is a pattern for Israel today: what is given to the Most High should cost the giver something.
precepts.why:
“Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing.” David would not offer to the Most High that which cost him nothing.

It is the same conviction in Chronicles. Ornan offered it all, the place, “the oxen also for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meat offering; I give it all.” But David said, “Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the Lord, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.” He paid six hundred shekels of gold, built the altar, and the Most High “answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering”, and the angel “put up his sword again into the sheath thereof.”

This is a pattern for Israel today: what is given to the Most High should cost the giver something.

precepts.text: The angel commanded David to set up an altar unto the Lord in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.
precepts.point: These are the things wherein Solomon was instructed for the building of the house of God: the length was threescore cubits, the breadth twenty cubits, and the porch in front was twenty cubits long according to the breadth of the house, and the height was a hundred and twenty. He overlaid it within with pure gold.
precepts.why:
“Then the angel of the Lord commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the Lord in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.” This is the threshingfloor read of a few days ago in First Chronicles 21.

That same ground is where Solomon built. He “began to build the house of the Lord at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the Lord appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.” The altar David set up at the angel’s command marked the place of the house of God.

Solomon began “in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign”, and these “are the things wherein Solomon was instructed for the building of the house of God”: threescore cubits long, twenty cubits broad, the porch twenty cubits by the breadth of the house, “and the height was an hundred and twenty: and he overlaid it within with pure gold.” Chronicles mixes here what is in First Kings 6 and 7, and Kings goes into much more detail on the building.

points: Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number the people; David commanded Joab to number Israel from Beersheba to Dan.
Joab objected, asking why the king would require this thing and be a cause of trespass to Israel, but the king's word prevailed.
Joab numbered the people: a thousand thousand and a hundred thousand men that drew sword in Israel, and four hundred threescore and ten thousand in Judah.
Joab left Levi and Benjamin uncounted because the king's word was abominable to him.
The Most High was displeased with the numbering and smote Israel; David confessed he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly and begged that the iniquity be taken away.
The Most High sent Gad the seer to offer David three choices: three years of famine, three months of destruction before his foes, or three days of pestilence with the destroying angel.
David chose to fall into the hand of the Most High rather than the hand of man, saying very great are His mercies, for he knew man would not show him the mercy the Most High would.

The Most High sent pestilence, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell; the angel was sent to destroy Jerusalem, but the Most High beheld it, repented of the evil, and told the angel it was enough to stay his hand.

David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the Most High standing between earth and heaven with a drawn sword stretched over Jerusalem, and he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces.
David pleaded that he alone had sinned by commanding the numbering, asking that the hand be on him and his father's house but not on the people, who as sheep had done nothing.
The angel commanded Gad to tell David to set up an altar in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, and David went up at the word spoken in the name of the Most High.

Ornan, threshing wheat, turned and saw the angel and hid with his four sons, then saw David and bowed to the ground; David asked to buy the threshingfloor for the full price so the plague might be stayed.
Ornan offered to give it all, the place, the oxen, the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat, but David refused to take what was another man's or to offer burnt offerings without cost.
David paid the full price rather than take the offering for free, and this is a pattern for Israel today: what is given to the Most High should cost the giver something.
David paid six hundred shekels of gold, built the altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the Most High answered him by fire from heaven and commanded the angel to sheathe his sword.
When David saw that the Most High answered him at the threshingfloor of Ornan, he sacrificed there.
The tabernacle Moses made and the altar of burnt offering were then at the high place in Gibeon.
David could not go to Gibeon to inquire of the Most High because he was afraid of the sword of the angel, so he worshipped at the new altar instead.
